title: Evals: a test set you can trust
summary: An eval is a fixed set of test cases, a grader and an honest statistic. Build cases from real traces, held apart from tuning. Grade with code where possible; validate an LLM judge against hand labels with Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance agreement. Put an error bar on every score with the bootstrap, compare versions with a paired bootstrap on the same cases, and turn every bug into a regression case through error analysis.
llm_link: Model outputs vary run to run, so a change that 'looks better' on five examples is noise until a measured eval says otherwise. Lesson 10.7 covered benchmark scores; this lesson is about evaluating your own application.
key_ideas: Eval = test cases + grader + statistic. Draw cases from real traces, cover hard and embarrassing ones, record what a good answer must contain, and keep them out of tuning.
Grade with code first (exact match, valid JSON, required citation, passing tests). Use an LLM judge with a rubric only after measuring its agreement with hand labels.
Cohen's kappa (1960): κ = (pₒ − pₑ)/(1 − pₑ), observed agreement corrected by the agreement expected by chance from each grader's label frequencies.
Bootstrap (Efron, 1979): resample the cases with replacement thousands of times; the middle 95% of the recomputed scores is a confidence interval.
Paired comparison: grade both versions on the same cases and bootstrap the per-case differences; an interval that includes zero means no demonstrated improvement.
Error analysis: read failures, group them, fix the biggest group, and add each new bug as a regression case.

quiz.q: Two graders label 100 answers pass/fail and agree on 90. Is that strong agreement?
options: Not necessarily: if both mark almost everything 'pass', they would agree often by chance alone, which kappa corrects for
quiz.explain: If each grader says 'pass' 95% of the time, chance agreement is 0.95² + 0.05² ≈ 0.905, so 90% observed agreement gives a kappa near zero.

quiz.q: Predict the result: two graders agree on 80% of cases, and chance agreement is 50%. What is Cohen's kappa?
quiz.explain: κ = (0.8 − 0.5)/(1 − 0.5) = 0.6: the graders achieved 60% of the agreement that was possible beyond chance.

quiz.q: What does one bootstrap resample consist of?
options: A new set of test cases written by hand
The same number of cases drawn from the test set with replacement, so some repeat and some are left out
The test set sorted by difficulty
quiz.explain: Recomputing the score on thousands of such resamples shows how much it could move by luck, which is what a confidence interval summarises.

quiz.q: Version B beats A by 2 points; the paired bootstrap interval for B − A is (−1.5, +5.5). What can you conclude?
options: Not yet shown: the interval includes zero, so the difference could be luck
quiz.explain: A 95% interval that includes zero means the data are consistent with no improvement. Add cases, or treat the change as neutral.

quiz.q: Why should eval cases come from your own production traces rather than a public benchmark?
options: They reflect what your users actually ask, including your product's specific hard cases, which a general benchmark does not cover
quiz.explain: A benchmark measures general ability; your eval must measure your application, on your users' distribution of requests.

problems.title: Bootstrap a confidence interval
problems.prompt:
Write bootstrap_ci(scores, n_boot=2000, seed=0, level=0.95). scores is a list of per-case scores (e.g. 1 for pass, 0 for fail).

  1. Make rng = random.Random(seed) so the result is reproducible.
  2. n_boot times: draw len(scores) scores with replacement (rng.choices) and record their mean.
  3. Sort the means and return the pair at positions int(tail * n_boot) and int((1 - tail) * n_boot) - 1, where tail = (1 - level) / 2.

tests.name: the interval contains the observed mean
tests.code:
s=[1]*140+[0]*60
lo,hi=bootstrap_ci(s)
assert lo<0.70<hi, f'the observed 0.70 should lie inside the interval, got ({lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f})'

tests.name: a sensible width for 200 cases
tests.code:
s=[1]*140+[0]*60
lo,hi=bootstrap_ci(s)
assert 0.08<hi-lo<0.18, f'with 200 cases at 70%, a 95% interval is about 0.13 wide, got {hi-lo:.3f}'

tests.name: more cases, narrower interval
tests.code:
lo1,hi1=bootstrap_ci([1]*35+[0]*15)
lo2,hi2=bootstrap_ci([1]*700+[0]*300)
assert (hi2-lo2)<(hi1-lo1)/2, f'20x more cases should shrink the width a lot: {hi1-lo1:.3f} vs {hi2-lo2:.3f}'

tests.name: no variation, no width
tests.code: assert bootstrap_ci([1]*50)==(1.0,1.0), 'if every case passes, every resample mean is 1.0'

hints: means = [sum(rng.choices(scores, k=n)) / n for _ in range(n_boot)]
return means[int(tail * n_boot)], means[int((1 - tail) * n_boot) - 1]
problems.solution:
import random

def bootstrap_ci(scores, n_boot=2000, seed=0, level=0.95):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(scores)
    means = sorted(sum(rng.choices(scores, k=n)) / n for _ in range(n_boot))
    tail = (1 - level) / 2
    return means[int(tail * n_boot)], means[int((1 - tail) * n_boot) - 1]

problems.title: Does the judge agree with you?
problems.prompt:
Write cohens_kappa(a, b) for two equal-length lists of labels (from you and from an LLM judge, say).

po = fraction of cases where a and b agree
pe = sum over labels c of  P(a says c) * P(b says c)
kappa = (po - pe) / (1 - pe)

Raise ValueError for lists of different lengths or empty lists, and return 1.0 when pe is 1 (both graders always use the same single label).

problems.title: Did the new prompt really help?
problems.prompt:
Write paired_diff_ci(old, new, n_boot=2000, seed=0, level=0.95). old and new are per-case scores of two versions on the same cases, in the same order.

Compute the per-case differences new[i] - old[i], then bootstrap their mean exactly as in the first problem. Return (mean_difference, lo, hi). Raise ValueError if the lists differ in length, because then the cases are not paired.

tests.name: a real improvement
tests.code:
old=[0]*30+[1]*70; new=[1]*30+[1]*70
m,lo,hi=paired_diff_ci(old,new)
assert abs(m-0.30)<1e-9 and lo>0, f'new fixes 30 cases and breaks none: mean 0.30, interval above 0; got ({m:.2f}, {lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f})'

tests.name: fixes one, breaks another: no proof
tests.code:
old=[1,0]*50; new=[0,1]*50
m,lo,hi=paired_diff_ci(old,new)
assert abs(m)<1e-9 and lo<0<hi, f'equal wins and losses: mean 0 and an interval around 0, got ({m:.2f}, {lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f})'

tests.name: a small edge on few cases is not shown
tests.code:
old=[1,1,0,1,0,1,1,0,1,1]; new=[1,1,1,1,0,1,0,1,1,1]
m,lo,hi=paired_diff_ci(old,new)
assert m>0 and lo<=0, f'10 cases with a 1-case edge cannot prove an improvement, got ({m:.2f}, {lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f})'

tests.name: unpaired input raises

hints: if len(old) != len(new): raise ValueError('not paired')
rng = random.Random(seed); means = sorted(sum(rng.choices(diffs, k=n)) / n for _ in range(n_boot))
return sum(diffs) / n, means[int(tail * n_boot)], means[int((1 - tail) * n_boot) - 1]
problems.solution:
import random

def paired_diff_ci(old, new, n_boot=2000, seed=0, level=0.95):
    if len(old) != len(new):
        raise ValueError("both versions must be graded on the same cases")
    diffs = [b - a for a, b in zip(old, new)]
    n = len(diffs)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    means = sorted(sum(rng.choices(diffs, k=n)) / n for _ in range(n_boot))
    tail = (1 - level) / 2
    return sum(diffs) / n, means[int(tail * n_boot)], means[int((1 - tail) * n_boot) - 1]
